title: Joshua Wong, heir to the Cold War dissidents
gist: Historian Jeffrey Wasserstrom compares jailed Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong to Soviet-bloc dissident Adam Michnik, arguing that cross-border activist friendships (Wong-Netiwit, Michnik-Haraszti-Havel) echo Cold War solidarity and that repressive outcomes are not permanent. Wong has been jailed over five years as of October 2026 and faces a new sentence.

insights.claim: Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong and Thai activist Netiwit Chotiphatphaisal, both born in 1996, built a cross-border friendship from 2016 based on a shared love of their home places and dislike of the Chinese Communist Party.
insights.speaker: Jeffrey Wasserstrom
insights.so_what: Pan-Asian activist networks exist and can be tracked as an indicator of regional resistance to Beijing.

insights.claim: The CCP is described as simultaneously transforming Hong Kong into a mainland-style city and backing Thailand's junta, which gives activists in both places a common adversary.
insights.speaker: Jeffrey Wasserstrom
insights.so_what: Beijing-backed political alignment in Southeast Asia is a shared grievance that can link protest movements across borders.
insights.locator: united by longing to improve a place they loved

insights.claim: Activists reciprocated in public: Netiwit joined a 2019 demonstration outside the Chinese Embassy in Bangkok, and Wong stood outside Hong Kong's Thai consulate in late 2020 to decry police brutality in Bangkok.
insights.speaker: Jeffrey Wasserstrom
insights.so_what: Pattern of mutual protest actions shows transnational coordination in Asia.

insights.claim: Joshua Wong was arrested before the end of 2020 on what the author calls trumped-up charges and, as of early October 2026, has spent more than five years continuously in jail, with another sentence expected imminently.
insights.speaker: Jeffrey Wasserstrom
insights.so_what: Signals continued tightening of the political environment in Hong Kong with no easing in sight.

insights.claim: Wong was sentenced for one alleged crime and then for another just before he was due to be released, implying a pattern of prolonging detention of prominent dissidents.
insights.speaker: Jeffrey Wasserstrom
insights.so_what: Rule-of-law risk in Hong Kong remains elevated for political figures.
insights.locator: sentenced first for one alleged crime

insights.claim: In a 2024 court appearance, his first chance in years to make a public statement, Wong shouted three words: 'I love Hong Kong.'
insights.speaker: Jeffrey Wasserstrom
insights.so_what: Illustrates that patriotism and political ideals are fused for the dissident, not separable.

insights.claim: Wong resembles Adam Michnik: both began activism young, were jailed before age 20 or in early adulthood by authorities taking cues from Moscow or Beijing, and refused exile; Michnik declined release conditional on leaving Poland after 1981.
insights.speaker: Jeffrey Wasserstrom
insights.so_what: Historical analogy frames Hong Kong repression as a recurrent authoritarian pattern rather than a unique event.

insights.claim: Miklos Haraszti told the author that Netiwit's trip to Hong Kong resembled his own 1970s trip to Poland to meet Michnik, which produced an enduring friendship and later collaborations such as Michnik-Havel.
insights.speaker: Jeffrey Wasserstrom
insights.so_what: Dissident friendships across borders historically seeded broader opposition networks.

insights.claim: When activists in one Soviet-bloc country were persecuted, friends in other countries gathered signatures for letters of support, a template for cross-border solidarity.
insights.speaker: Jeffrey Wasserstrom
insights.so_what: Solidarity networks are a leading indicator of how external pressure on authoritarian states is mobilised.
insights.locator: gathered signatures for letters of support

themes.theme: Why repression may not be permanent

insights.claim: A Cold War-era reviewer wrote in 1986 that communist rule would still be uncelebrated in 1995; he was wrong, as unexpected changes occurred and a Czech friend of Michnik's went from playwright to president by 1995.
insights.speaker: Jeffrey Wasserstrom
insights.so_what: Forecasts of durable authoritarian stability have a poor historical record; keep tail scenarios of regime change in view.
insights.locator: He was wrong. Unexpected changes occurred.

insights.claim: Michnik's early-1980s prison letters argue for treasuring memories of camaraderie and bravery even from failed movements, and finding ways to keep despair at bay in dark times.
insights.speaker: Jeffrey Wasserstrom
entities: Letters from Prison and Other Essays
insights.so_what: Morale and memory are treated as resources for long-horizon resistance.
insights.locator: treasure memories of camaraderie and bravery
